reference.title: Band Incline Chest Press
reference.listing: Video (movement reference; the page could not be fetched from the authoring environment (proxy refused gymvisual.com), so the data sheet was not read; the movement is taken from the exercise name and standard coaching practice)

breathing.pattern: Breathe out as you press forward and up, breathe in as the band draws the hands back.
breathing.cadence: About 1 s press, short hold, about 2 s back

prescription.tempo: 2-0-1-0 (2 s down, no pause, 1 s up)
prescription.load: Band tension is user-chosen (bands are colour-coded by tension): pick one you can move for the target reps with 1-3 reps in reserve; stand or sit farther from the anchor, or choke up on the band, for more tension.
prescription.progression: More reps, a slower return, more distance from the anchor (more stretch), then the next band up.

cues.text: Loop a band around each upright of a rack behind you, a little below shoulder height. Staggered stance, knees soft, ribs down; a handle in each hand beside the chest, palms down, elbows back and out about 45-60 degrees.
Breathe out and press forward and up, about 30 degrees above horizontal, until the arms are nearly straight.
Hands about forehead height in front, shoulders down; do not let the band pull the trunk back.
Breathe in and let the hands come back to the chest slowly along the same line.
Brief pause at the chest with the band still taut, then press again.

mistakes.mistake: Leaning back or arching the low back as the band tightens
mistakes.fix: Ribs down, glutes lightly braced, weight over the front foot; use a lighter band.

mistakes.mistake: Shrugging the shoulders up toward the ears at the top
mistakes.fix: Reach forward and up but keep the shoulders down.

mistakes.mistake: Elbows flared straight out at 90 degrees
mistakes.fix: Keep the elbows about 45-60 degrees from the body.

mistakes.mistake: Letting the band snap the hands back

kinematics.norm: Hands travel forward and up about 30 degrees above horizontal, the angle of a 30-degree incline press, which gave the highest upper-pectoralis activity on the bench (Rodríguez-Ridao 2020, barbell; clinical opinion for the standing band version)
About 90-110 degrees at the chest to nearly straight at the top (clinical opinion)
About 45-60 degrees from the body at the chest, not a 90-degree "T" (clinical opinion)

Anchored behind, a little below the shoulders, so it resists the forward-and-up press; tension is highest at the top. Elastic resistance can give muscle activity comparable to free weights (Andersen 2010; Calatayud 2015, band push-ups vs bench press)
Staggered stance, knees soft, so the band does not pull you backward (clinical opinion)
Controlled, about 1 s press and 2 s return (clinical opinion)

sources.title: GymVisual, Band Incline Chest Press, video (movement reference)

Rodríguez-Ridao, Antequera-Vique, Martín-Fuentes and Muyor 2020, effect of five bench inclinations on the electromyographic activity of the pectoralis major, anterior deltoid and triceps brachii during the bench press exercise (Int J Environ Res Public Health 17(19):7339; PMC7579505)

Andersen, Andersen, Mortensen, Poulsen, Bjørnlund and Zebis 2010, muscle activation and perceived loading during rehabilitation exercises: comparison of dumbbells and elastic resistance (Phys Ther 90(4):538-549)

Calatayud, Borreani, Colado, Martin, Tella and Andersen 2015, bench press and push-up at comparable levels of muscle activity results in similar strength gains (J Strength Cond Res 29(1):246-253; elastic-band push-ups)

Saeterbakken, van den Tillaar and Fimland 2011, a comparison of muscle activity and 1-RM strength of three chest-press exercises with different stability requirements (J Sports Sci 29(5):533-538; PubMed 21225489)

cautions: Check the band for nicks or tears before every session and replace a worn band; a band that snaps can hit the face or eyes.
Anchor the band to something that cannot move or slip (a rack upright, a heavy bench frame or under the feet) and make sure it is secure before loading it.
Band tension rises as it stretches, so the load is lightest at the start and heaviest at the end of the push; let it return under control rather than snapping back.
Shoulder pain: shorten the range at the chest (clinical opinion).
Stop if sharp pain, numbness or tingling occurs.
Muscle glow colours and activation curves are illustrative, not measured EMG.
modify: Shoulder discomfort: palms facing each other and the elbows a little more tucked.
regressions: Lighter band or step closer to the anchor.
progressions: Stronger band or step farther from the anchor.
Slower 3 s return with a pause at the chest.
Band incline bench press or incline dumbbell press.

muscleNotes.pec_r: Main pusher, with a shift toward the upper (clavicular) fibres: a 30-degree incline gave the highest upper-pectoralis activity, while the middle and lower fibres fell as the bench was raised (Rodríguez-Ridao 2020, barbell); Lauver 2016 also recommends a 30-degree incline for the pectoralis major.
muscleNotes.pec_l: Main pusher, with a shift toward the upper (clavicular) fibres: a 30-degree incline gave the highest upper-pectoralis activity, while the middle and lower fibres fell as the bench was raised (Rodríguez-Ridao 2020, barbell); Lauver 2016 also recommends a 30-degree incline for the pectoralis major.
muscleNotes.ant_deltoid_r: Works harder as the bench rises: at 30 degrees it was about as active as the upper chest, and it became the most active muscle at 45 and 60 degrees (Rodríguez-Ridao 2020).
muscleNotes.ant_deltoid_l: Works harder as the bench rises: at 30 degrees it was about as active as the upper chest, and it became the most active muscle at 45 and 60 degrees (Rodríguez-Ridao 2020).
muscleNotes.triceps_r: Straightens the elbows; triceps activity did not change with bench angle (Rodríguez-Ridao 2020) and is lower with dumbbells than with a barbell (Saeterbakken 2011).
muscleNotes.triceps_l: Straightens the elbows; triceps activity did not change with bench angle (Rodríguez-Ridao 2020) and is lower with dumbbells than with a barbell (Saeterbakken 2011).
muscleNotes.serratus_r: Holds the shoulder blades against the rib cage while each arm moves on its own.
muscleNotes.serratus_l: Holds the shoulder blades against the rib cage while each arm moves on its own.
muscleNotes.biceps_r: Works as a stabiliser: biceps activity rose with the stability demand, highest with dumbbells (Saeterbakken 2011).
muscleNotes.biceps_l: Works as a stabiliser: biceps activity rose with the stability demand, highest with dumbbells (Saeterbakken 2011).
muscleNotes.infraspinatus_r: Rotator cuff: centres the head of the upper arm while the band handles move freely (clinical opinion).
muscleNotes.infraspinatus_l: Rotator cuff: centres the head of the upper arm while the band handles move freely (clinical opinion).
muscleNotes.rhomboids_midtrap_r: Keep the shoulder blades drawn back and down on the bench.
muscleNotes.rhomboids_midtrap_l: Keep the shoulder blades drawn back and down on the bench.
muscleNotes.core: Keeps the trunk upright so the band does not pull it back or arch the low back (clinical opinion).
